docs.title: Software Management & Development
docs.text:
IE University · MFT & MCSDI · Term 1, 2026–27

In this course you build real software, from an empty laptop to an application running in the cloud. In fifteen sessions you will set up a professional development environment, write a Python backend with a database and a REST API, put a web frontend on top of it, test it, package it in containers, and deploy it to Microsoft Azure. Along the way you will learn the habits that make software teams work: version control, code review, reproducible environments, and small, frequent deliveries.

Every session follows the same pattern. First, a short explanation of the ideas (why the tool exists and what problem it solves). Then a lab where you apply them, step by step, to one application that grows during the course.

docs.title: The application we build: a personal ledger
docs.text:
The running example is ledger, a small fintech application that records accounts and transactions and computes balances and spending by category. It starts in session 3 as a 30-line Python script that reads a CSV file. It ends in session 14 as a three-part system running on Azure: a web dashboard, a REST API and a PostgreSQL database.

 S3–S6   laptop:  python script ──▶ structured package
 S7–S10  laptop:  frontend ──▶ FastAPI ──▶ PostgreSQL (in Docker)
 S11–S12 laptop:  the same three parts, in Docker Compose
 S13–S14 Azure:   Static Web Apps ──▶ Container Apps ──▶ PostgreSQL

Your group project follows the same path with an application of your own choosing (a budgeting tool, a portfolio tracker, an invoicing system…). Whatever you learn in a lab on the ledger, you then apply to your project.

docs.title: Local first, then the cloud
docs.text:
We build everything on your own machine first. You run the database and the services yourself, with Docker, so you understand every part and can break and repair it at no cost. Only then do we move to the cloud. There, managed services do the same jobs for us, and we pay for them.

We use Microsoft Azure. The syllabus describes the cloud part with Google Cloud names. The concepts are the same, and this is the equivalent we use:

docs.title: Using AI
docs.text:
Generative AI is encouraged in this course. Professional developers use AI assistants every day, and you should learn to use them well. Three rules:

  1. You are responsible for every line you submit. Assume AI output is wrong until you have run it and understood it. In the exam and in the live demo, you will be asked to explain your code.
  2. Acknowledge it. State which tool you used, for what, and with which prompts, as the syllabus describes. Acknowledging AI use does not lower your grade.
  3. Learn the fundamentals first. AI makes a developer who understands the basics much faster. A developer who doesn't understand them, it makes much slower at debugging. The labs are designed for you to type the commands and read the errors yourself.

docs.title: Environments and reproducibility
docs.text:
What you need first

Nothing. This is the first page of the course.

docs.title: "It works on my machine"
docs.text:
Picture a small fintech team. Ana writes a Python script that reads the day's card transactions and flags suspicious ones. It works perfectly on her laptop. She sends it to Ben, who runs the overnight jobs, and on his machine it fails in four different ways in one afternoon:

  1. It crashes immediately: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'. Ana installed pandas months ago and forgot about it.
  2. Ben installs pandas, and the script crashes again with a syntax error on a line that uses match. Ana has Python 3.12; the server has Python 3.9, which doesn't know that keyword.
  3. Ben upgrades Python, and the script runs but cannot find C:\Users\ana\Desktop\cards.csv. That path exists only on Ana's Windows laptop; the server runs Linux.
  4. Ben fixes the path and the script finishes, but it flags almost nothing. Ana's laptop had an environment variable, RISK_THRESHOLD=0.8, set in her shell profile. On the server the script fell back to its default of 0.99.

None of these failures is a bug in the logic Ana wrote. They are all differences between her machine and Ben's. Each one took time to diagnose, and the last one is the most dangerous: the script seemed to work. In a real company, the fourth failure could let fraud through for weeks.

This is why software teams care so much about environments. The code is only one part of what runs. The rest is everything around it, and it has to be the same, or at least known, everywhere the code runs: on each developer's laptop, on the test server and in production.

docs.title: What an environment is made of
docs.text:
We can describe everything around the code as a stack of layers. Each layer is built on the one below it, and each one can cause a failure like Ana's.

Definition: development environment

The environment of a program is everything, apart from its own source code, that determines how it runs. From the bottom up:

  1. Hardware: above all, the processor architecture (x86_64, also called amd64, on most Windows PCs and servers; arm64, also called aarch64, on Apple Silicon Macs and many cloud servers).
  2. Operating system: its kernel (the core that manages memory, processes and devices: Linux, Windows NT, Darwin on macOS) and its userland (the basic programs and libraries around the kernel).
  3. System packages: programs and libraries installed on the OS (git, curl, a PostgreSQL client, the SSL libraries…).
  4. Language runtime: the interpreter or compiler, with its version (Python 3.14, Node 22…).
  5. Project dependencies: the third-party libraries the code imports, with their versions (pandas 2.3, fastapi 0.120…).
  6. Configuration: environment variables, configuration files, secrets (passwords and API keys).
  7. External services: everything the program talks to over the network: databases, other APIs, file storage.

In Ana's story, the failures came from layers 5 (pandas missing), 4 (Python version), 2 (Windows paths on Linux) and 6 (the threshold variable). The table below gives an example of a bug for every layer. Use it as a checklist when something "works on my machine":

Layer Typical "works on my machine" failure Hardware A library ships compiled code only for x86_64, and installation fails on an arm64 Mac Operating system Paths with \ instead of /; file names that differ only in capitals (Data.csv and data.csv are the same file on macOS and Windows, but different files on Linux) System packages The code calls git or psql, and they aren't installed on the server Runtime New syntax (match, type aliases) or new standard modules (tomllib) on an old Python Dependencies A different version of a library changes a default or removes a function Configuration A variable set on one machine but not on another, as in Ana's story External services The test database has different data, or a different version, than production

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The remedy is to make environments reproducible.

Definition: reproducible environment

An environment is reproducible if anyone, on any supported machine, can rebuild it from written instructions or files and get the same result: the same versions of everything, the same configuration and therefore the same behaviour of the code.

The key words are from files. If the environment exists only as "what I happened to install on my laptop over two years", nobody can rebuild it, not even its owner after a hard-disk failure. The practical rule is that the environment should be described in files that live with the code, in the same repository.

There are three levels of ambition, and professional teams usually combine all three:

  1. Document it. A README that lists what to install and how. It is better than nothing, but people skip steps and instructions go out of date.
  2. Automate it. Files that tools read to install exactly what is needed. In Python that is pyproject.toml with a lockfile (uv.lock), which pins the exact version of every dependency (session 3). The configuration goes into an .env file, which is not committed, and a template of it, which is (session 12).
  3. Package it. Ship the environment itself together with the code: a virtual machine image or a container image that already contains the operating system, the runtime and the dependencies (sessions 11–14).

Each level covers more layers of the stack. A README can't stop someone from installing the wrong Python. A lockfile fixes layer 5, and with a tool like uv also layer 4. A container image fixes layers 2 to 5 at once.

docs.title: Three places to run software: host, virtual machine, container
On the host
docs.text: The simplest option is to install everything directly on your computer, the host. Python, PostgreSQL and the libraries go on the operating system you use every day. It is fast and nothing stands between the program and the machine. The price is that every project shares the same system. Project A needs PostgreSQL 15 and project B needs 17; one upgrade breaks the other. After a year, nobody knows exactly what is installed or why.

docs.title: Virtual machines
docs.text:
A virtual machine (VM) is a complete computer simulated in software. A program called a hypervisor (VirtualBox, UTM, VMware, Hyper-V, Parallels) divides the real hardware into virtual CPUs, memory and disks. On those, it boots a whole second operating system, the guest OS. You can run Ubuntu inside your Mac or Windows laptop, with its own kernel, its own users and its own installed software. If you break it, you delete it and create it again.

VMs give strong isolation: each guest is a separate computer, and the guest can be a different OS from the host. The cost is weight. Each VM runs a full operating system, takes gigabytes of disk and a fixed slice of RAM, and takes tens of seconds to boot.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A container isolates a program without simulating a computer. Every container on a machine shares the host's kernel. The kernel itself keeps containers apart. Each one gets its own view of the filesystem, its own processes and its own network (Linux namespaces), and limits on how much CPU and memory it can use (cgroups). Inside, the container only needs the program and its libraries, not a whole OS.

A container starts from an image: a read-only package with the filesystem the program needs (for example, a minimal Ubuntu userland plus Python plus your code). From one image you can start as many containers as you want, and they will all be identical. The most common tool for building and running them is Docker (session 11).

Definition: virtual machine and container

  • A virtual machine emulates a complete computer. It runs its own operating system, kernel included, on virtual hardware provided by a hypervisor.
  • A container is an isolated group of processes that shares the host's kernel. It sees only the files of its image, its own processes and its own network.

The difference has practical consequences:

Host Virtual machine Container What is isolated nothing the whole computer processes, files, network Own kernel — yes no, shares the host's Start-up time — tens of seconds under a second Size — gigabytes megabytes to a few hundred MB Runs a different OS — yes (Windows on a Mac, Linux on Windows…) only the same kind of kernel: Linux containers need a Linux kernel Typical use your daily tools a full, separate workstation or server packaging and shipping one application

That "Linux containers need a Linux kernel" line explains something that surprises many people. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows runs a small Linux VM in the background, and your containers run inside it. On Windows, that VM is usually the one from WSL2 (the Windows Subsystem for Linux). So on a laptop the two technologies are stacked: a VM that provides the Linux kernel, and containers on top. On a Linux server there is no VM in between, and containers run directly on the host kernel.

docs.title: Processor architectures
docs.text:
There is one layer that neither VMs nor containers make disappear: the processor. A program compiled for x86_64 contains machine instructions that an arm64 processor does not understand, and the other way round. Python code is portable, but many Python libraries (NumPy, the PostgreSQL driver, cryptography) include compiled parts, and they are published separately for each architecture.

This matters in this course in two places:

  • Your laptop. Apple Silicon Macs (M1 to M5) are arm64. Most Windows laptops are x86_64, but Windows on ARM (Snapdragon processors) is becoming common. You will see these names in installers: choose the right one.
  • Shipping to the cloud. A container image built on an arm64 Mac is, by default, an arm64 image. Many cloud services expect x86_64 (linux/amd64). If you push the wrong one, the deployment fails with an error like exec format error. In session 13 we will build images for the right platform explicitly.

Emulation can run code for the other architecture (Rosetta 2 on Macs, QEMU in Docker), but it is slower and sometimes fragile. It is useful in an emergency, but not something to rely on.

docs.title: From your laptop to the cloud
docs.text:
Everything so far runs on a machine you own: your laptop, or a server in your company's data centre. This is called on-premises ("on-prem"): you own the hardware and you are responsible for every layer of the stack.

Cloud computing means renting those layers from a provider (Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud) and paying for what you use. Different services take more or less of the stack off your hands:

Model You manage The provider manages Example in Azure On-premises everything nothing — IaaS (infrastructure as a service) OS, runtime, dependencies, app, data hardware, network, virtualization Azure Virtual Machines PaaS / serverless containers your container image (app + dependencies) and its configuration everything below, plus scaling Azure Container Apps Managed services your data and settings the whole service Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Static Web Apps SaaS (software as a service) only how you use it everything Microsoft 365, GitHub

As you move down the table you control less, but you also have less to patch, monitor and keep running at 3 a.m. This is the main trade-off in the cloud. What is still yours is your code, its dependencies and its configuration. That is exactly the part a container packages. The container is the unit that travels from your laptop to the cloud unchanged, and that is why the course spends three sessions on it.

The cloud has costs of its own. It is billed by usage, and a forgotten resource keeps billing. Your data lives in someone else's data centre, which matters for regulated industries like finance (where the data is stored, who can access it). And every service is a little different from its equivalent at another provider. We will meet all three issues in sessions 13 and 14.

docs.title: The course map
docs.text:
The whole course follows one application, ledger, through this stack:

Sessions Where it runs What you add 1–2 your laptop a known, reproducible working environment 3–6 your laptop, on the host a Python project with locked dependencies, under version control, well structured 7–10 your laptop, with PostgreSQL in a container a database, a REST API, tests and a web frontend 11–12 your laptop, all in containers the three services in Docker Compose, configured from the environment 13–14 Azure the same images, running on managed cloud services

The movement is from left to right in the table of the previous section, from on-premises toward managed services. At every step you will know exactly what is underneath, because you first ran it yourself.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• "A container is a lightweight VM." It looks like one from the inside, but it has no kernel of its own. This is why it starts in milliseconds, and also why it cannot run a different kind of operating system than the host.
  • "It runs in Docker, so it runs everywhere." Only on the same architecture, or under emulation. Check the platform of your images.
  • "I'll remember how I set it up." You won't, and your teammates can't read your memory. If it isn't in a file in the repository, it isn't reproducible.
  • Confusing environment and configuration. The configuration (layer 6) is one part of the environment. It is the part that should differ between your laptop and production (a different database, different keys). Everything else should be the same.

Key takeaways

  • A program's environment is everything except its own code: hardware, operating system, system packages, runtime, dependencies, configuration and external services. A difference in any layer can break it.
  • An environment is reproducible when it can be rebuilt from files that live with the code: documentation, then automation (lockfiles), then packaging (images).
  • A VM emulates a whole computer with its own kernel. A container isolates processes but shares the host kernel, so it is far lighter. On Mac and Windows, Docker runs containers inside a small Linux VM.
  • The processor architecture (arm64 or x86_64) is part of the environment. Images must be built for the platform where they will run.
  • The cloud models (IaaS, PaaS, managed services, SaaS) differ in which layers you manage. The container image is the part that is yours in every model, and the unit that travels from laptop to cloud.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. For each failure, name the layer of the environment that causes it: (a) pip install fails with "no matching distribution" on a new Mac but works on a colleague's Windows laptop; (b) the app connects to the test database instead of the production one; (c) import tomllib fails with ModuleNotFoundError; (d) the script works on the developer's Mac but cannot find Config.yaml on the Linux server, where the file is called config.yaml.

Solution
  • (a) Hardware (architecture): the library has a compiled package for x86_64 but not for arm64. If no version for your platform exists, pip has nothing to install.
  • (b) Configuration: the database address comes from a setting or environment variable that points to the wrong place. The services are fine; the configuration chooses the wrong one.
  • (c) Runtime: tomllib is part of the standard library only from Python 3.11. The code runs on an older Python.
  • (d) Operating system: macOS file systems are case-insensitive by default, so Config.yaml finds config.yaml. Linux is case-sensitive, so it doesn't.

2. A colleague says: "Our app runs in Docker, so we don't need to pin library versions in pyproject.toml; the image already contains them." Is that right?

Solution

Only half right. The image freezes the versions that were installed when it was built. But the image is rebuilt from the Dockerfile every time someone changes the code. If the dependencies aren't pinned, each rebuild can install newer versions, and two images built a week apart can behave differently. The lockfile makes the build reproducible; the image makes the result portable. You need both.

3. You need to: (a) try a Linux command-line tool for an afternoon without installing anything on your Windows laptop; (b) run the same API in ten identical copies to handle more traffic; (c) test how your company's software installs on a fresh Windows 11 machine. For each case, would you choose a VM or a container? Why?

Solution
  • (a) A container: docker run -it ubuntu gives you a disposable Linux shell in a second, and nothing remains when you exit. A VM would also work, but it is much heavier for an afternoon.
  • (b) Containers: starting ten copies from the same image is fast and cheap, and they are identical by construction. This is exactly what services like Azure Container Apps do.
  • (c) A VM: you need a complete Windows operating system, kernel included, in a clean state. A container shares the host's kernel, so it can't give you a fresh Windows.

4. Ana builds a container image on her M3 MacBook and deploys it to a cloud service that runs x86_64 servers. The deployment fails with exec format error. Explain what happened and how she can avoid it.

Solution

Her Mac is arm64, so by default Docker built an arm64 image: the Python interpreter and every compiled library inside it contain ARM instructions. The cloud server's processor is x86_64, cannot execute them, and the kernel refuses with exec format error. She must build the image for the target platform, linux/amd64 (with Docker, docker build --platform linux/amd64 …), or let the image be built by a CI service that runs on x86_64. We do both in session 13.

5. A bank wants to run its new customer-facing API. Option A: buy servers for its own data centre. Option B: Azure Virtual Machines. Option C: Azure Container Apps. For each option, list two things the bank's team must still manage, and give one reason a bank might still choose option A.

Solution
  • A, on-premises: everything, for example the physical hardware and its replacement, and the operating system updates (plus networking, power, physical security…).
  • B, IaaS: the operating system (patches, security updates) and the runtime and dependencies installed on it, plus scaling: deciding how many VMs to run.
  • C, serverless containers: the container image (the app, its dependencies, the base image's security updates) and its configuration and secrets. Scaling is configured, not managed by hand.
  • Why choose A: regulation or data-residency rules that require full control of where customer data lives and who can touch the hardware. Others are an existing investment in its own data centre, or predictable, constant loads, which can be cheaper on hardware it owns than on pay-per-use.

docs.title: Development environments
docs.text:
Software never runs in a vacuum. Your Python script runs on an interpreter, which runs on an operating system, which runs on a particular kind of processor. The script also reads files, connects to a database and expects some settings to be there. When any of these pieces changes, the same code can behave differently or not run at all. This first session is about that whole stack, the development environment: what it is made of, why teams work so hard to make it identical for everyone, and which tools they use to do so (virtual machines, containers and the cloud).

It is also the session where we get to know your machine. The rest of the course depends on it.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Environments and reproducibility. What an environment is, layer by layer, and why "it works on my machine" is one of the most expensive sentences in software. Then the three tools for making environments reproducible (host installation, virtual machines and containers) and where the cloud fits in. It ends with a map of what we will build during the course.
  2. Lab 1: know your machine. You open a terminal, find out exactly what your laptop is (operating system, processor architecture, memory, disk), create your GitHub account, and write it all down on a machine card. You need that card in session 2 to set up the course environment.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • List the layers of a development environment and give an example of a bug caused by each one.
  • Explain the difference between running software on the host, in a virtual machine and in a container, and when each one is the right choice.
  • Explain why the processor architecture (arm64 or x86_64) matters when you run and ship software.
  • Describe what changes when an application moves from your laptop to the cloud, and who is responsible for each layer in each case.
  • Open a terminal on your computer and find its operating system, architecture, memory and free disk space.

docs.text: You need no prior knowledge. Bring your laptop charged and make sure you know your password: you will need it to install software in the coming sessions.

docs.title: Lab 1: know your machine
docs.text:
What you need first

Your laptop, with its password, and your IE email. The concepts are in Environments and reproducibility.

In this lab you meet the tool you will use more than any other in the course, the terminal. You use it to find out exactly which environment your laptop provides, layer by layer. You also create the GitHub account we need from session 5 onwards. Before you start, download the machine card and write your answers in it as you go: in session 2 you use it to set up the course environment, so fill it in carefully.

You don't install anything today. Every command below only reads information.

docs.title: 1. Open a terminal
docs.text:
A terminal is a window where you type commands as text, and a program called the shell runs them and prints the result. Every operating system has one:

macOSWindowsLinux

Press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and press Enter. The shell on recent macOS versions is zsh.

Press the Win key, type Terminal and open Windows Terminal (on Windows 10, if you don't have it, open Windows PowerShell). The shell is PowerShell.

Press Ctrl+Alt+T, or look for Terminal in your applications. The shell is usually bash.

You see a prompt: a short line ending in %, $ or >, followed by a blinking cursor. Type the command after it and press Enter. In this course, a command block shows only what you type. Don't type the prompt symbol.

Start with three commands that work in all three shells:

whoami
pwd
ls

whoami prints your user name. pwd (print working directory) prints the folder the shell is "in", which is your home directory when you open a terminal. ls lists the files in it.

What you should see

Your user name, then a path to your home folder, then its contents (Desktop, Documents, Downloads…). The path depends on the system:

  • macOS: /Users/<you>
  • Windows: C:\Users\<you>
  • Linux: /home/<you>

Note the separators: / on macOS and Linux, \ on Windows. This is the operating-system layer of the environment, and you can already see it.

docs.title: 2. Identify the operating system and the architecture
docs.text:
Now go up the stack from the bottom, starting with the processor architecture and the operating system. Use the tab for your system:

macOSWindowsLinux 
sw_vers
uname -m

sw_vers prints the macOS version. uname -m prints the machine architecture.

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version
$env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE

The first command prints the Windows edition (Home, Pro, Enterprise…) and version. The second prints the processor architecture.

cat /etc/os-release
uname -m

/etc/os-release is a text file that describes the distribution. cat prints it.

What you should see
  • macOS: ProductName: macOS, a version such as 26.6, and then arm64 (Apple Silicon: M1, M2…) or x86_64 (older Intel Macs).
  • Windows: a caption such as Microsoft Windows 11 Pro and a version such as 10.0.26100 (Windows 11 still reports itself as version 10.0 internally). Then AMD64 (an Intel or AMD processor, the x86_64 architecture) or ARM64 (a Snapdragon processor).
  • Linux: the name and version of your distribution (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS…), and x86_64 or aarch64 (the Linux name for arm64).

The same architecture has several names: x86_64 = amd64 = AMD64, and arm64 = aarch64 = ARM64. You will see all of them in installers and in Docker.

docs.title: 3. Memory, disk and virtualization
docs.text:
Containers, databases and VMs need memory and disk space. Write down how much you have:

macOSWindowsLinux 
echo $(( $(sysctl -n hw.memsize) / 1073741824 )) GB
df -h ~

sysctl -n hw.memsize returns the memory in bytes; dividing by 1073741824 (2³⁰) converts it to GB. df -h ~ shows the disk that holds your home folder: look at the Avail column.

Virtualization is always available on Macs, so there's nothing more to check.

[math]::Round((Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).TotalPhysicalMemory / 1GB)
Get-PSDrive C
wsl --status

The first line prints the memory in GB, and Get-PSDrive C prints the used and free space of the C: drive, in GB. wsl --status tells you whether the Windows Subsystem for Linux is installed. If it isn't, it prints a message saying so, which is fine.

To check that virtualization is enabled, open the Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), go to Performance → CPU and look for Virtualization: Enabled under the graph.

free -h
df -h ~

free -h shows the memory: look at the total column of the Mem: row. df -h ~ shows the free space under Avail.

What you should see

Something like 16 GB of memory and a free-space figure. For the course you need at least 8 GB of memory (16 GB is comfortable) and at least 20 GB of free disk. If you have less, don't worry: write it down on your machine card. Session 2 has setup options for smaller machines.

On Windows, if Virtualization says Disabled, write that down too: it can be turned on in the computer's firmware settings (BIOS/UEFI), and we will help you with that in session 2.

docs.title: 4. Can you install software?
docs.text:
Many professionals bring a laptop managed by their employer, with restrictions on what they can install. These restrictions can make Docker or a VM impossible, so we need to know now.

Answer these questions for yourself:

  • Is this laptop yours, or does it belong to your employer?
  • When you install an application, does the system ask for your password (you are an administrator), or for an IT department's approval?
  • Is there corporate security software that blocks installations or manages the device (a "device management" profile on macOS, a company account in Windows settings)?
macOSWindowsLinux

This command prints admin if your user is an administrator, and nothing otherwise:

id -Gn | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -x admin

Open Settings → Accounts → Your info. Under your name it says Administrator or Standard user. Under Settings → Accounts → Access work or school you can see whether the laptop is connected to an organization.

This command prints sudo if you can run administrator commands:

groups | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -x sudo

docs.title: 5. Create your GitHub account
docs.text:
GitHub hosts your code from session 5 onwards and runs our automated pipelines in session 13. Create the account now, because verifying it can take a while. If you already have one, use it.

  1. Go to github.com/signup and create an account. Choose a professional username: it appears in your repositories, and employers will see it on your CV.
  2. Enable two-factor authentication (Settings → Password and authentication). GitHub requires it to contribute code.
  3. Optionally, apply to the GitHub Student Developer Pack with your IE email. It gives you free access to GitHub Copilot and other developer tools.

When you finish, upload your filled-in machine card to the Session 1: Machine Card assignment on Blackboard. Keep a copy: you need it in session 2.

Download the template (.md)

docs.title: Linux and the shell
docs.text:
Almost all the software you will deploy in your career runs on Linux. That includes the servers behind banking apps, the containers in this course and the machines that run Azure Container Apps. Almost all of it is set up and operated from a shell: a text interface where you type commands. Graphical interfaces come and go, but the shell is the same on your laptop, in a container and on a server on the other side of the world, and it is the only interface many of those machines have.

This session gives you a working knowledge of both: how a Unix system is organized, and how to get things done in its shell. It is also the session where everybody sets up the course environment, using the machine card you filled in during session 1.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. The shell and the filesystem. The Unix philosophy (small tools that do one thing, combined with pipes), how the filesystem is organized, and the twenty or so commands that cover most daily work.
  2. Users, packages and the environment. Who can do what (users, groups, permissions, sudo), how software is installed (package managers), and the environment variables that configure every program, starting with PATH.
  3. Setting up the course environment. The setup we use for the rest of the course, with installation steps for each operating system.
  4. Lab 2: a ledger in the shell. You create the project folder for the course application, download its first dataset, answer questions about the transactions with pipelines, and write your first shell script.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • Navigate the filesystem with absolute and relative paths, and create, copy, move and delete files and folders from the shell.
  • Answer simple questions about a text file by combining grep, cut, sort, uniq, wc and awk with pipes and redirections.
  • Read and change file permissions, and explain when and why to use sudo.
  • Install software with your system's package manager.
  • Explain what an environment variable is, set one for a command or for a session, and diagnose a "command not found" error with PATH.
  • Have the course environment installed and working.

docs.title: Lab 2: a ledger in the shell
docs.text:
What you need first

The course environment installed and checked (Setting up the course environment). The commands are explained in The shell and the filesystem and Users, packages and the environment.

In this lab you create the folder for ledger, the application we build during the course. You download its first data, a CSV file with three months of transactions from a personal checking account and a savings account, and answer questions about the money using only the shell. Then you turn your best pipeline into a script, the first piece of code of the project.

Type the commands rather than copying them: the point is to get them into your fingers. Use Tab to complete names.

docs.title: 1. Create the project folder
docs.text:
All the course work goes into one folder, smd, in your home directory. Inside it, create the folder for the application and a data folder for its data:

cd ~
mkdir -p smd/ledger/data
cd smd/ledger
pwd
What you should see

pwd prints the absolute path of the new folder: /Users/<you>/smd/ledger on macOS, /home/<you>/smd/ledger on Linux, WSL and the VM, /workspaces/... in a codespace (where the course repository already gives you a working folder; create ledger inside it).

mkdir -p created the three nested folders in one go. Run the same command again: -p doesn't complain when they already exist.

docs.title: 2. Download the data
docs.text:
curl downloads a URL. -o saves the result to a file instead of printing it, and -fsSL makes curl fail clearly on errors (-f), stay quiet (-s) but still show errors (-S), and follow redirects (-L):

curl -fsSL -o data/transactions.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ami232/ie-smd/main/data/transactions.csv
ls -l data

Look at the first lines and count them:

head -n 5 data/transactions.csv
wc -l data/transactions.csv
What you should see 
date,account,description,category,amount
2026-01-01,checking,Rent,housing,-950.00
2026-01-02,checking,Carrefour,groceries,-65.15
2026-01-03,checking,Spotify,subscriptions,-11.99
2026-01-05,checking,Netflix,subscriptions,-13.99

and 57 data/transactions.csv: a header line plus 56 transactions. Each row has a date, the account (checking or savings), a description, a category and a signed amount in euros. Spending is negative, income positive.

Use less data/transactions.csv to scroll through the whole file (Q to quit). What happens at the end of each month?

docs.title: 3. Questions with grep
docs.text:
How many grocery purchases are there? grep keeps the matching lines, and -c counts them instead of printing them:

grep -c groceries data/transactions.csv

Now, how many times did the account holder shop at Mercadona? Try it with and without -i (ignore case):

grep mercadona data/transactions.csv
grep -i mercadona data/transactions.csv

Finally, show only the movements of the savings account. Searching for savings alone would also match Transfer to savings in the checking account. Include the commas to match the whole column:

grep ",savings," data/transactions.csv
What you should see
  • 12 grocery purchases.
  • grep mercadona prints nothing, because the file says Mercadona with a capital M. With -i, three purchases appear (16 January, 10 February and 16 March).
  • Six movements in savings: each month a 300.00 transfer from checking and a small interest payment.

docs.title: 4. Spending by category
docs.text:
Which categories have the most transactions? This is the sort | uniq -c | sort -rn pattern from the concepts page, applied to the fourth column. tail -n +2 skips the header line:

cut -d, -f4 data/transactions.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Build the pipeline one step at a time. Run cut -d, -f4 data/transactions.csv alone, then add | tail -n +2 and run it again, then | sort, and so on. Look at what each step does to the lines. That is how you write and debug pipelines.

What you should see 
  12 groceries
  11 restaurants
   9 transport
   6 transfer
   6 subscriptions
   3 interest
   3 income
   3 housing
   3 health

The number of spaces at the start of each line may vary between systems.

docs.title: 5. Sums with awk
docs.text:
Counting is not enough for a ledger: we need amounts. awk splits each line into fields (-F, uses the comma as separator, $5 is the fifth field) and can add them up. NR > 1 skips the first line (NR is the line number) and the END block runs after the last line:

awk -F, 'NR > 1 { total += $5 } END { printf "%.2f
", total }' data/transactions.csv

The total of every row combined is the net change across both accounts. Now compute the total spent on restaurants by filtering first with grep:

grep ",restaurants," data/transactions.csv | awk -F, '{ total += $5 } END { printf "%.2f
", total }'

(No NR > 1 here: grep already removed the header.)

What you should see

4255.10 for the net total, and -320.09 for restaurants: 320.09 euros spent in three months.

printf "%.2f " prints the number with two decimals. Without it, awk would print 4255.1. In session 3 you will see that adding money with ordinary floating-point numbers can give results like 4255.099999999999, and how Python avoids it.

docs.title: 6. Save results to a file
docs.text:
Use redirection to build a small report:

echo "Transactions per category" > report.txt
cut -d, -f4 data/transactions.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn >> report.txt
cat report.txt

The first line creates the file (>) and the second appends (>>). Change the second >> to > and run both again: what happens to the title?

docs.title: 7. Your first script
docs.text:
Commands you need more than once belong in a script: a text file of commands. Create balance.sh, which prints the balance of each account. The cat > file <<'EOF' … EOF construction writes everything up to the EOF line into the file. Type or paste the whole block at once:

cat > balance.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prints the balance of each account in a transactions CSV.
file="${LEDGER_FILE:-data/transactions.csv}"
echo "Balances in $file"
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { s[$2] += $5 } END { for (a in s) printf "%-10s %10.2f\n", a, s[a] }' "$file" | sort
EOF

Line by line:

  • #!/usr/bin/env bash, the shebang, tells the system to run the file with bash.
  • file="${LEDGER_FILE:-data/transactions.csv}" reads the environment variable LEDGER_FILE and, if it isn't set, uses the default path. This is how programs get their configuration, as described in the concepts page.
  • The awk program adds the amounts per account. s[$2] is a table indexed by the second column.

Now run it:

./balance.sh

It fails. Look at the permissions, fix them and run it again:

ls -l balance.sh
chmod +x balance.sh
ls -l balance.sh
./balance.sh
What you should see

The first attempt gives permission denied: ./balance.sh (zsh) or bash: ./balance.sh: Permission denied (bash): a new file is not executable. ls -l shows -rw-r--r--. After chmod +x it shows -rwxr-xr-x, and the script prints:

Balances in data/transactions.csv
checking      3349.10
savings        906.00

docs.title: 8. Configure it with an environment variable
docs.text:
Make a file with only the checking account's movements, and point the script at it for one command:

grep -v ",savings," data/transactions.csv > data/checking.csv
LEDGER_FILE=data/checking.csv ./balance.sh
./balance.sh

Then export a file that doesn't exist, run the script and check its exit code:

export LEDGER_FILE=data/missing.csv
./balance.sh
echo $?
unset LEDGER_FILE
What you should see

With LEDGER_FILE=data/checking.csv, only the checking line appears: grep -v kept all the lines except the savings ones (the header included). The next ./balance.sh uses the default file again, because the variable existed only for that one command.

With the missing file, awk prints an error saying it can't open data/missing.csv, yet echo $? prints 0: the script says it succeeded. Exercise 5 of the concepts page explains why, and how set -o pipefail fixes it. Add set -euo pipefail as the second line of balance.sh and try again. Now the exit code is not 0.

docs.title: 9. Install a tool with the package manager
docs.text:
Install tree, which draws a folder as a tree:

macOSUbuntu (WSL, VM, codespace) 
brew install tree

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y tree

Then look at your project:

cd ~/smd
tree
which tree
What you should see 
.
└── ledger
    ├── balance.sh
    ├── data
    │   ├── checking.csv
    │   └── transactions.csv
    └── report.txt

which tree prints /opt/homebrew/bin/tree on an Apple Silicon Mac and /usr/bin/tree on Ubuntu. Those are two folders in your PATH, where each package manager puts its programs.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
You have finished the lab when:

  • ~/smd/ledger contains data/transactions.csv, report.txt and an executable balance.sh;
  • ./balance.sh prints the two balances (3349.10 and 906.00);
  • you can explain, without looking, what each command of the category pipeline in step 4 does.

Challenge (optional). Write a pipeline that prints the total spent per category, from the most to the least. Count only negative amounts, and leave out transfers, which move money between your own accounts but don't spend it. Hint: in awk, the condition can combine tests with && ($5 < 0 && $4 != "transfer"). Use a table indexed by $4, as in balance.sh, then sort the output by its second column, numerically, with sort -t' ' -k2 -n.

Result to check

With spending as negative numbers, sorting numerically puts the biggest spending first:

housing -2850.00
groceries -797.60
restaurants -320.09
transport -135.57
health -119.70
subscriptions -77.94

docs.title: Setting up the course environment
docs.text:
What you need first

Your "machine card" from Lab 1, administrator rights on your laptop and a good internet connection. The downloads add up to a few gigabytes, most of it Docker. The ideas behind the options are in Environments and reproducibility.

For the rest of the course, everybody needs the same three things: a Unix shell (bash or zsh), a package manager to install tools, and Docker to run containers. You install all three today: first the shell and the package manager, which are all that Lab 2 needs, and then Docker, which we use from session 7 onwards. Installing it now leaves time to fix any problem before then. There are several ways to get them, and the right one depends on your laptop: keep the machine card from Lab 1 at hand. Your instructor announces the setup for the class.

This page describes the three possible setups, which we call tracks. Follow the one announced in class, unless your instructor tells you individually to use another one.

Track What you get Who it suits A. Native your own OS's terminal + Docker Desktop (on Windows, a real Ubuntu through WSL) most laptops: 16 GB of memory or more, administrator rights B. Ubuntu VM an Ubuntu server running in a VM on your laptop, with Docker inside when you want everything isolated from your own system, or native Docker doesn't work C. Cloud a Linux machine in GitHub Codespaces, used from the browser or VS Code managed laptops without administrator rights, low-spec machines, tablets

Whichever track you follow, the commands in the rest of the course are the same: you always work in a Linux-style shell.

docs.title: Track A: native
docs.text:
macOSWindowsLinux

macOS is already a Unix system, and its Terminal runs zsh, so you only need a package manager and Docker.

Install Homebrew, the package manager for macOS. Paste the command from brew.sh into the Terminal:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

It asks for your password and installs Apple's command-line developer tools if you don't have them (that takes a few minutes). At the end it prints "Next steps": two commands that add Homebrew to your PATH. Run them. Then check:

brew --version

On Windows, we work inside WSL (the Windows Subsystem for Linux): a real Ubuntu, with bash and apt, integrated with Windows. Docker Desktop uses it too.

What WSL is

WSL lets Linux programs run on Windows without dual booting and without managing a VM yourself. Its current version, WSL 2, runs a real Linux kernel, built by Microsoft, inside a small, lightweight virtual machine that Windows starts and stops for you in a second or two. On top of that kernel you install a distribution (we use Ubuntu), which brings the usual Linux userland: bash, apt and the standard tools.

Unlike a VM you create yourself, WSL is integrated with Windows. Ubuntu appears as a tab in Windows Terminal; the Windows disk is visible from Linux at /mnt/c; your Linux files are visible from the File Explorer under Linux; and Windows programs (such as VS Code) can work on Linux folders. Docker Desktop uses the same lightweight VM to run Linux containers, which is why it needs WSL.

The older WSL 1 had no Linux kernel: it translated Linux system calls into Windows ones. It was slower for files and couldn't run Docker. wsl --install installs WSL 2.

1. Install WSL with Ubuntu. Right-click Terminal (or PowerShell) and choose Run as administrator. Then run:

wsl --install

This enables the virtualization components, installs the Linux kernel and the Ubuntu distribution. Restart Windows when it finishes.

If WSL is already installed with another distribution (or only with docker-desktop), wsl --install doesn't add Ubuntu. Run wsl --install -d Ubuntu instead. wsl --list --verbose shows what you have.

2. Create your Linux user. After the restart, open Ubuntu from the Start menu (it also appears as a tab in Windows Terminal). The first time, it asks for a user name and password for Linux. They are independent of your Windows account; choose something you'll remember, because sudo will ask for this password. Then update the system:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Work inside Ubuntu, not in PowerShell

From now on, open the Ubuntu terminal for the course and keep your projects in your Linux home folder (~, which is /home/<you>), not in /mnt/c/.... Files on the Windows disk are much slower to access from Linux, and their permissions behave differently.

If wsl --install fails, the most common cause is virtualization being disabled in the firmware (Lab 1, step 3). Ask your instructor.

You already have the shell and the package manager: only Docker is left.

docs.title: Track B: an Ubuntu VM
docs.text:
We use Multipass, a tool from Canonical (the company behind Ubuntu) that creates Ubuntu VMs with one command, on macOS, Windows and Linux. You work in the VM through its shell.

1. Install Multipass. On macOS: brew install --cask multipass (install Homebrew first, as in track A). On Windows or Linux, download it from canonical.com/multipass. On Windows Home, Multipass needs VirtualBox, and the installer explains how to set it up.

2. Create the course VM with 2 CPUs, 4 GB of memory and 30 GB of disk, and open a shell in it:

multipass launch 24.04 --name smd --cpus 2 --memory 4G --disk 30G
multipass shell smd

The prompt changes to ubuntu@smd:~$: you are now inside the VM. Everything else in the course happens here.

Useful commands, run on your laptop (not inside the VM): multipass list (VMs and their state), multipass stop smd (frees the memory when you're not working) and multipass start smd.

docs.title: Track C: GitHub Codespaces
docs.text:
A codespace is a Linux machine in GitHub's cloud, with VS Code in the browser and Docker ready to use. Nothing is installed on your laptop. A personal GitHub account includes a free monthly quota (enough for about 60 hours on the smallest machine), and the GitHub Student Developer Pack raises it.

  1. Sign in to GitHub. Your instructor gives you the link to the course's starter repository.
  2. In the repository, click Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  3. After a minute, VS Code opens in the browser. The Terminal panel at the bottom is a bash shell on Ubuntu.

Stop your codespace when you finish

A codespace consumes your quota while it runs. It stops on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, but it's better to stop it yourself: on github.com/codespaces, … → Stop codespace.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Install Docker once your shell works: on Windows, Docker Desktop needs WSL with Ubuntu, so finish the steps above first. Docker needs about 20 GB of free disk for the program and the images, and on a Mac a recent macOS: Docker Desktop supports the current version and the two previous ones.

Not enough space, or an older macOS?

Skip Docker today and tell your instructor. Free space or update macOS before session 7, the first session that uses Docker. Everything else today, Lab 2 included, works without it.

macOSWindowsLinuxUbuntu VM (track B)Codespace (track C)

Install Docker Desktop. Download it from docker.com/products/docker-desktop. Choose Apple Silicon or Intel according to the architecture on your machine card. Open the .dmg, drag Docker to Applications and start it. Accept the terms. You can skip signing in.

Install Docker Desktop. Download it from docker.com/products/docker-desktop (choose ARM64 if your machine card says ARM64) and install it with the default options, which use WSL 2. Start it, then in Settings → Resources → WSL integration turn on the integration with Ubuntu.

Install Docker Engine following the official instructions for your distribution (docs.docker.com/engine/install). Then let your user run Docker without sudo:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Log out and in again for the group change to take effect.

Inside the VM (multipass shell smd), install Docker from Ubuntu's own packages and let your user use it:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y docker.io docker-compose-v2
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
exit

exit leaves the VM. Run multipass shell smd again so that the group change takes effect.

Docker is already installed.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Whatever your track, open the course shell (macOS Terminal, the Ubuntu terminal on Windows, multipass shell smd, or the codespace terminal) and run:

echo $SHELL
uname -sm
curl --version | head -n 1
docker run --rm hello-world
What you should see
  • /bin/zsh or /bin/bash.
  • Darwin arm64 (or Darwin x86_64) on a Mac. Linux x86_64 or Linux aarch64 everywhere else: in WSL, in the VM and in a codespace you are on Linux.
  • A line starting with curl 8. (any version is fine).
  • Docker downloads a tiny image and prints a message that starts with Hello from Docker! and explains what just happened.

If docker says permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket, your user isn't in the docker group yet: log out and in again (or exit and reopen the VM shell). If it says Cannot connect to the Docker daemon, Docker Desktop isn't running: start it.

Once the first three commands work, you're ready for Lab 2. The Docker check can wait until after the lab if Docker is still downloading.

docs.title: The shell and the filesystem
docs.text:
What you need first

A terminal open on a Unix shell: macOS Terminal, Linux, WSL on Windows or an Ubuntu container. Lab 1 shows how to open one. Try every command on this page as you read: the shell is learned with the fingers.

docs.title: Why a text interface
docs.text:
Suppose your manager asks: how much did we spend on restaurants last quarter, and with which merchant the most? The transactions are in a CSV file. With a spreadsheet you open it, filter a column, select cells, read the sum, sort another column. It works, but there is no record of what you did, and next quarter you do it all again by hand.

In the shell, the same question is one line:

grep ",restaurants," transactions.csv | cut -d, -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

   5 Rodilla
   4 La Tagliatella
   2 Five Guys

You can read the line from left to right. It keeps the restaurant rows, takes the third column (the merchant), sorts it, counts repeated values and sorts by the count. The line is the record of what you did. You can save it, share it, run it again next quarter, or run it on a server that has no screen at all. That is the reason the shell has survived fifty years of graphical interfaces: commands are text, and text can be saved, repeated, combined and automated.

docs.title: Terminal, shell and other words
docs.text:
A few words appear constantly in this course, and they are often used loosely. The two most often confused are terminal and shell, and they are different programs. The terminal is the window: it shows text and sends what you type to the program running inside it. The shell is the program inside the window that reads your command, runs it and prints the result. A useful comparison is a phone call: the terminal is the phone, and the shell is the person on the other end who carries out your requests. You can change one without the other. macOS Terminal, Windows Terminal and the terminal panel in VS Code are all terminals, and any of them can run zsh, bash or PowerShell.

Word What it means Examples Terminal (terminal emulator) the window where you type text and read the output macOS Terminal, Windows Terminal, the VS Code terminal Shell the program that reads your commands and runs them zsh, bash, PowerShell Command line, CLI working by typing commands, as opposed to a graphical interface (GUI). A CLI tool is a program meant to be used this way git, docker, uv Prompt the text the shell prints when it is waiting for a command ana@laptop ~ %, ubuntu@smd:~$ Command one instruction: a program name plus its options and arguments ls -la data Console historically, the physical screen and keyboard of a computer. Today mostly a synonym of terminal Script a text file of commands that the shell runs one after another balance.sh Process a program while it is running. Every command you type starts at least one Working directory the folder the shell is "in" right now. Relative paths start from it /home/ana/smd Home folder your personal folder, written ~ /home/ana, /Users/ana Kernel the core of the operating system: it manages memory, processes, files and devices Linux, Darwin (macOS) Unix the operating system from the 1970s whose design Linux and macOS follow, which is why their shells work the same way Linux, distribution Linux is strictly a kernel. A distribution packages it with a shell, tools and a package manager into a complete system Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora

When this course says "open a terminal", it means: open the terminal window, where a Unix shell (zsh or bash) shows you its prompt.

docs.title: The Unix philosophy
docs.text:
Unix, the operating system Linux and macOS descend from, was designed around a few ideas that still explain how the shell works:

  • Each program does one thing well. sort sorts lines. wc counts them. grep keeps the lines that match a pattern. None of them tries to do everything.
  • Programs work together. The output of one is the input of the next. A program doesn't care whether its input comes from a file, the keyboard or another program.
  • Text is the universal interface. Programs read and write lines of plain text, so any program can be combined with any other.

The grep … | cut … | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn line above is this philosophy in action: five tiny programs, each trivial, combined into an analysis.

docs.title: Anatomy of a command
docs.text:
Every command has the same shape:

ls -l -h /etc
  • ls is the command: the program to run.
  • -l and -h are options (or flags). They change how the command behaves: here, long format with human-readable sizes. Short options can be combined (ls -lh). Long options start with two dashes (ls --all).
  • /etc is an argument: what the command acts on.

Spaces separate the parts. A file name with spaces must be quoted, "my file.csv", or the shell sees two arguments. This is one reason why developers avoid spaces in file names.

When a command finishes, it returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means an error. You rarely see it, but scripts and automated pipelines depend on it. echo $? prints the exit code of the last command.

docs.title: One tree
docs.text:
On Windows, each disk has its own letter (C:\, D:\). On Unix systems there is a single tree that starts at the root, written /. Every file, every disk, even every device hangs somewhere below it. The main folders follow a convention, the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, which is why any Linux server feels familiar:

Folder What it contains / the root of the tree /home/<user> each user's personal files (on macOS, /Users/<user>) /root the home of the administrator user, root /etc system-wide configuration files (text files, by tradition) /usr/bin, /bin programs available to all users /usr/local/bin programs installed by hand, outside the package manager /var/log logs: what services report while they run /tmp temporary files, deleted on reboot /proc, /sys not real files: a view into the running kernel (Linux only)

You will meet these folders again. In session 11, a container image is exactly a tree like this one, packed into a file.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
A path says where a file is in the tree:

  • An absolute path starts at the root: /home/ana/smd/ledger/data/transactions.csv. It means the same thing wherever you are.
  • A relative path starts from the current directory, the folder the shell is in now: if you are in /home/ana/smd, then ledger/data/transactions.csv refers to the same file.

Three shortcuts appear in paths all the time:

Symbol Means ~ your home directory (/home/ana) . the current directory .. the parent directory, one level up

So ../data means "the data folder next to the one I'm in", and ./balance.sh means "the balance.sh in this folder".

Definition: current directory and paths

Every shell has a current (working) directory, printed by pwd and changed with cd. An absolute path starts with / (or ~) and is resolved from the root (or home). A relative path is resolved from the current directory.

docs.title: Moving around
docs.text:
Command Does pwd prints the current directory ls lists the files here (ls -la: all files, including hidden ones, with details) cd folder goes into folder cd .. goes up one level cd or cd ~ goes home cd - goes back to the previous directory

Files whose names start with a dot (.env, .git, .bashrc) are hidden: ls doesn't show them unless you add -a. Many configuration files are hidden this way, so remember -a when "the file isn't there".

docs.title: Working with files
docs.text:
Command Does mkdir -p a/b/c creates folders (-p: including missing parents, no error if they exist) touch file.txt creates an empty file (or updates its date) cp src dst copies (cp -r for folders) mv src dst moves or renames rm file deletes a file (rm -r folder for a folder) cat file prints a whole file less file shows a long file page by page (Q to quit, / to search) head -n 5 file, tail -n 5 file the first or last lines

There is no recycle bin

rm deletes immediately and for good. rm -r deletes a folder and everything inside it. Read an rm command twice before pressing Enter, and never run rm -rf with a path you have not checked.

docs.title: The three standard streams
docs.text:
Every program starts with three channels already open:

  • standard input (stdin): where it reads from, by default the keyboard;
  • standard output (stdout): where it writes its results, by default the terminal;
  • standard error (stderr): where it writes error messages, also the terminal by default.

Together they are called standard I/O, or stdio (you'll meet the name in documentation and in C's stdio.h). Each stream also has a number: 0 for stdin, 1 for stdout and 2 for stderr. You'll see the 2 again in the redirection 2>.

Why keep errors apart from results? Because results are often data that another program or a file will consume. If ls data nofile > list.txt wrote its complaint about nofile into list.txt, the error would end up mixed with the file names, and you wouldn't see it. With a separate stderr, the file gets only the listing and the error still appears on your screen.

The shell can reconnect these channels before the program starts. This is what makes the combination of small tools possible.

docs.title: Redirection
docs.text:
Syntax Does cmd > file sends stdout to file, replacing its contents cmd >> file appends stdout to the end of file cmd < file reads stdin from file cmd 2> file sends stderr to file cmd > file 2>&1 sends both stdout and stderr to file

For example, ls -l /etc > listing.txt saves the listing in a file instead of printing it.

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
A pipe, |, connects the stdout of one program to the stdin of the next:

ls /usr/bin | wc -l

ls writes the list of programs, one per line, and wc -l counts the lines it receives. Nothing is written to disk in between, and both programs run at the same time.

Definition: pipeline

A pipeline a | b | c runs the commands together, connecting the standard output of each one to the standard input of the next. Only the output of the last one reaches the terminal (or a file, if redirected).

docs.title: The text toolbox
docs.text:
These are the tools you combine in pipelines most often. Each reads lines from a file or from stdin:

Command Does Example grep pattern keeps lines containing pattern (-i: ignore case, -v: keep lines that don't match, -c: count) grep -i error app.log cut -d, -f3 keeps a column: here the 3rd, splitting on , cut -d, -f1,5 data.csv sort sorts lines (-n numerically, -r reversed) sort -rn uniq -c collapses adjacent repeated lines and counts them (so sort first) uniq -c sorted.txt wc -l counts lines wc -l data.csv head, tail first or last lines (tail -n +2: everything from line 2, which skips a header) tail -f app.log follows a log live awk a small language for columns: filters and sums awk -F, '{ s += $5 } END { print s }'

Here is the analysis from the start of the page again. Read each step as a transformation of lines:

grep ",restaurants," transactions.csv |   # only restaurant rows
  cut -d, -f3 |                           # only the merchant column
  sort |                                  # equal merchants become adjacent
  uniq -c |                               # count each merchant
  sort -rn                                # biggest count first

A line that ends in | continues on the next one, so long pipelines can be split and commented like this in a script. When you type in the terminal, write it on one line without the comments. (The interactive zsh of macOS doesn't accept # comments by default.)

docs.title: Help, history and shortcuts
docs.text:
Nobody remembers every option. These save a lot of time:

  • man grep opens the manual of grep (Q to quit). grep --help prints a shorter summary.
  • Tab completes file and command names. Type cd Doc and press Tab. Pressing it twice lists the options. Use it constantly: it is faster and it avoids typos.
  • Up and Down browse previous commands. Ctrl+R searches the history. history lists it.
  • Ctrl+C stops the running command. Ctrl+L (or clear) clears the screen.

docs.title: bash, zsh and PowerShell
docs.text:
bash is the standard shell on Linux and the one you will find on servers and in containers. zsh is the default on macOS. For everything in this course it behaves like bash. Both follow the same Unix conventions, and so does everything on this page.

PowerShell, on Windows, is a different design. Its commands pass objects instead of text, and many names differ (Get-ChildItem is its ls, although it accepts ls as an alias). It is a good shell, but it is not what your servers and containers run. That is why, on Windows, we work inside WSL, a real Linux with bash (Setting up the course environment).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Typing the path relative to the wrong place. If a "file not found" makes no sense, run pwd and ls: you are probably in another folder.
  • Spaces in names. cd My Documents tries to enter My. Quote it (cd "My Documents") or use Tab, which adds the quotes for you.
  • > instead of >>. > replaces the file. The previous contents are gone.
  • uniq without sort. uniq only merges adjacent duplicates. Unsorted input gives wrong counts without any error.
  • Copying commands from the web without reading them. Especially anything with sudo, rm or curl … | sh. Read it first.

Key takeaways

  • The shell runs commands (command -options arguments). Each returns an exit code, where 0 means success.
  • Unix has one filesystem tree starting at /. Paths are absolute (from /) or relative (from the current directory), and ~, . and .. are shortcuts.
  • Programs read stdin and write stdout and stderr. Redirection (>, >>, <, 2>) connects them to files, and pipes (|) connect programs.
  • Small tools (grep, cut, sort, uniq, wc, awk) combined in pipelines answer real questions about text files, and the pipeline itself documents the analysis.
  • Tab, the history and man make you fast. rm makes you careful.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. You are in /home/ana/smd/ledger/data. Write the absolute path and the shortest relative path to (a) /home/ana/smd/ledger/balance.sh; (b) /home/ana/smd/notes.txt; (c) /etc/hosts.

Solution
  • (a) Absolute: /home/ana/smd/ledger/balance.sh. Relative: ../balance.sh (one level up).
  • (b) Absolute: /home/ana/smd/notes.txt. Relative: ../../notes.txt (two levels up). Also ~/smd/notes.txt, which works from anywhere.
  • (c) Absolute: /etc/hosts. A relative path would be ../../../../../etc/hosts (up to the root and down again). It works, but the absolute path is obviously better: use relative paths for things near you.

2. What does each command do? (a) sort data.csv > data.csv; (b) grep -v "^#" config.txt | wc -l; (c) tail -n +2 data.csv | cut -d, -f1 | sort | uniq | wc -l.

Solution
  • (a) A classic trap: it empties data.csv. The shell opens the file for writing (and truncates it) before sort starts, so sort reads an empty file. To sort a file in place, write to another file and rename it, or use sort -o data.csv data.csv.
  • (b) Counts the lines of config.txt that do not start with # (^ means "start of line"), that is, the lines that aren't comments.
  • (c) Skips the header line, takes the first column, and counts how many distinct values it has. For a transactions file whose first column is the date, that is the number of days with at least one transaction.

3. Write a pipeline that prints the five most frequent words in a file report.txt, assuming there is one word per line.

Solution 

sort report.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5
sort puts equal words together, uniq -c counts them, sort -rn puts the biggest counts first and head -n 5 keeps five. This pattern, sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head, is worth memorizing: it answers "what is most frequent" for any column of any file.

4. A colleague runs uniq -c categories.txt and gets groceries counted several times on different lines, each time with a small number. What went wrong?

Solution

uniq only merges adjacent identical lines. The file wasn't sorted, so the groceries lines were scattered and each run of consecutive lines was counted separately. The fix is sort categories.txt | uniq -c.

5. Explain the difference between ls > out.txt, ls >> out.txt and ls | wc -l > out.txt.

Solution
  • ls > out.txt writes the listing to out.txt, replacing whatever was there.
  • ls >> out.txt adds the listing at the end of out.txt, keeping the previous contents.
  • ls | wc -l > out.txt sends the listing through wc -l, and only its result, the number of files, goes into out.txt (replacing it). The redirection applies to the last command of the pipeline.
